subject: security
title: Web Application Security
summary: How browsers isolate sites and how attackers get around that isolation: the same-origin policy and CORS, XSS and Content Security Policy, and CSRF with SameSite cookies.

lessons.title: The same-origin policy and CORS
lessons.summary: Why your browser stops one site reading another site's data, exactly what counts as an origin, and how CORS grants controlled access and how misconfiguration exposes data.
lessons.body: You are logged into your bank in one tab and reading a dodgy blog in another. Your browser holds the bank's session cookie. If the blog's JavaScript could simply `fetch("https://bank.example/api/balance")` and read the reply, every site you visited could read every other site you were logged into. The **same-origin policy** (SOP) is the browser rule that stops this. It is the foundation that almost all of web security sits on, so the rest of this module keeps coming back to it. ## What an origin is For ordinary HTTP(S) URLs, an **origin** compares the normalised **scheme, host and port**; an explicit default port and its omitted form are equivalent. Documents can instead have opaque origins, including sandboxed documents without same-origin permission. Identical `null` serialisations do not make distinct opaque origins equal. | URL (vs `https://shop.example`) | Same origin? | |---|---| | `https://shop.example/cart` | Yes (path ignored) | | `http://shop.example` | No: scheme | | `https://api.shop.example` | No: host | | `https://shop.example:8443` | No: port | The path, query string and fragment play no part. A subdomain is a different origin, even though it feels like "the same site". For the domain-based HTTP(S) examples here, a looser idea, the **schemeful site**, is the scheme plus the *registrable domain* (the "eTLD+1", such as `shop.example` or `example.co.uk`). `https://api.shop.example` and `https://www.shop.example` are **cross-origin but same-site**. Origins govern who can *read* what; sites govern when cookies are sent (the SameSite rules in lesson 3). Keep the two apart. ## What the SOP actually blocks A common misconception is that the SOP stops cross-origin *requests*. Mostly it does not. It stops cross-origin *reads*. ``` evil.example page bank.example | fetch(/api/balance) | |-------------------------->| request | (cookies attached) | is SENT |<--------------------------| | response arrives, but | | JS may NOT read it | ``` The diagram assumes a simple request using `credentials: "include"` and a cookie eligible under SameSite and browser policy; default cross-origin `fetch` omits cookies. Roughly, cross-origin interactions fall into three groups: - **Writes are usually allowed.** Links, redirects and HTML form submissions can target any origin. This is why CSRF (lesson 3) is possible. - **Embedding is usually allowed.** ``, `

questions.prompt: Which of these URLs is **same-origin** with `https://shop.example/home`?

options.text: `http://shop.example/home`
options.explanation: The scheme differs (`http` vs `https`). Origin includes the scheme, so this is cross-origin even though host and path match.

options.text: `https://shop.example/admin?x=1`
options.explanation: Correct. Scheme, host and (default) port 443 all match. Path and query string are not part of the origin.

options.text: `https://www.shop.example/home`
options.explanation: `www.shop.example` is a different host. Subdomains are separate origins, although they are the same *site*.

options.text: `https://shop.example:8443/home`
options.explanation: An explicit port 8443 differs from the implicit 443, so the origin differs. Port is part of the triple.

questions.workedExample:
Write each URL as (scheme, host, port) and compare with (https, shop.example, 443):

| URL | Triple | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| A | http, shop.example, 80 | No |
| B | https, shop.example, 443 | Yes |
| C | https, www.shop.example, 443 | No |
| D | https, shop.example, 8443 | No |

Only B matches on all three. The path `/admin` and query `?x=1` are ignored.

questions.prompt: A page on `https://evil.example` runs `fetch("https://bank.example/transfer", {method: "POST", body: "to=x"})`. The bank sends no CORS headers. Assume no CSP or other sending restriction and a reachable server. What does CORS itself do?

options.text: The browser refuses to send the request at all
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. A `POST` with a form-style body is a simple request, so it is sent without any preflight. The SOP blocks reading the response, not sending it.

options.text: The simple request can be sent, but the script cannot read the response without CORS permission
options.explanation: Correct. This simple request needs no preflight. The server may accept or reject it; absent CORS permission the response is not exposed. Default fetch credentials mode omits cross-origin cookies.

options.text: The request is sent, and the script can read the response because it was a POST
options.explanation: The method does not grant read access. Only a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header does.

options.text: The server rejects it automatically because the Origin header is foreign
options.explanation: Servers do nothing with `Origin` unless their code checks it. The SOP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

questions.workedExample: The string body gives a safelisted text/plain content type, and this POST has no unsafe author-set headers. Under the stated assumptions the browser sends it without preflight, but default cross-origin fetch does not include bank cookies. The server decides whether any action is authorised. Without allow-origin permission the CORS fetch rejects; it does not expose response contents. CSRF still matters for requests that carry eligible ambient credentials or otherwise cause an unauthorised action.

questions.prompt: What does CORS fundamentally do?

options.text: It lets a server tell browsers which other origins may read its responses, relaxing the same-origin policy
options.explanation: Correct. CORS is an opt-in relaxation: the server grants read access to named origins via response headers.

options.text: It protects an API from requests made by scripts on other sites
options.explanation: CORS is not a server-side firewall. Simple requests are still delivered, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely.

options.text: It encrypts cross-origin traffic between browser and server
options.explanation: Encryption is TLS's job. CORS is just a set of HTTP headers that control browser read access.

options.text: It stops a page from embedding cross-origin images and scripts
options.explanation: Classic no-cors embedding may work, but CORS-enabled images, module scripts and other resource modes can require CORS approval. Embedding also depends on CSP, CORP/COEP and framing policy.

questions.workedExample: CORS grants browser response-sharing permission and controls preflight approval for non-safelisted requests. Simple requests can still be sent without permission to read the response, while failed required preflights can prevent the actual request. Non-browser clients are not bound by browser CORS enforcement. The server must authenticate and authorise independently.

questions.prompt: A SPA makes CORS fetches to another origin, with no cached preflight permission. Assume safelisted header values where named, no extra author-set headers, no streaming body or upload-listener trigger, and no other sending restriction. Which need an OPTIONS preflight? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET /items with only Accept: application/json
options.explanation: GET with safelisted headers is a simple request; no preflight.

options.text: `POST /items` with `Content-Type: application/json`
options.explanation: Correct. `application/json` is not one of the three safelisted content types, so it needs a preflight.

options.text: `DELETE /items/3`
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied empty-cache conditions. DELETE is not a CORS-safelisted method.

options.text: `GET /me` with an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header
options.explanation: Correct. `Authorization` is not a CORS-safelisted header, so even a GET is preflighted.

options.text: `POST /upload` with `multipart/form-data`
options.explanation: `multipart/form-data` is safelisted (an HTML form can send it), so this is a simple request.

questions.workedExample: Under these assumptions, GET with a safelisted Accept value and POST with a safelisted multipart content type avoid preflight. JSON content type, DELETE and the Authorization header require permission and therefore OPTIONS with an empty preflight cache. Header lengths/bytes and API-specific flags matter too; a header name alone is not the complete safelist test.

questions.prompt:
An API responds to a credentialed `fetch` (with `credentials: "include"`) from `https://app.example` like this:

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

What does the browser do?

options.text: Lets the script read the response, since `*` matches every origin
options.explanation: The wildcard is specifically forbidden for credentialed requests. Treating `*` as "matches everything" here is the misconception.

options.text: Lets the script read the response but strips the cookies
options.explanation: Credentials mode include does not guarantee any eligible cookie exists or is sent. The wildcard fails the CORS credentials-mode check regardless; stripping cookies from an already received response is not the rule.

options.text: Blocks the response: with credentials, the origin must be named exactly
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests, so the fetch fails with a CORS error.

options.text: Sends a second preflight asking for the exact origin
options.explanation: There's no automatic retry. The request simply fails, and the developer must fix the server's headers.

questions.workedExample: With credentials mode include, the CORS check cannot use wildcard allow-origin, even when no cookie is eligible. An allowed named origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required to expose the response. Eligible cookies remain subject to SameSite and browser policy. For dynamically selected origins preserve Vary: Origin, and separately prevent shared caching of private user data.

options.text: `https://example.com.evil.net`
options.explanation: This ends in `evil.net`, not `example.com`, so `endswith` returns False. (A `startswith` or `in` check would fall for it.)

options.text: `https://evilexample.com`
options.explanation: Correct. The suffix comparison accepts that string although its hostname is not example.com or its subdomain. The question assumes attacker control; actual domain registration availability is irrelevant.

options.text: None: `endswith` is a safe suffix check
options.explanation: A suffix check without a leading dot accepts any domain whose name merely ends in those letters.

options.text: `null`
options.explanation: The string `"null"` does not end in `example.com`, so this check rejects it, though an allowlist that included `null` would be a separate bug.

questions.workedExample:
Evaluate `endswith("example.com")` on each:

```
https://evilexample.com     True
https://example.com.evil.net False
null                        False
```

The fix is an exact set lookup:

```python
ALLOWED = {"https://example.com",
           "https://app.example.com"}
ok = origin in ALLOWED
```

Even `endswith(".example.com")` would trust every subdomain, including forgotten ones with XSS bugs.

questions.prompt: Your API correctly reflects allowlisted origins in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` but omits `Vary: Origin`. A CDN caches responses. What can go wrong?

options.text: Nothing, because CORS headers are evaluated by the browser, not the CDN
options.explanation: The browser evaluates them, but the CDN decides which stored copy (with which header) to hand back. That is the problem.

options.text: The cache may reuse origin A's allow-origin header for origin B, causing B's CORS check to fail
options.explanation: Correct if the shared cache does not otherwise vary on Origin. Its key may include other dimensions; omission does not imply URL-only caching.

options.text: Preflights stop working because OPTIONS cannot be cached
options.explanation: Preflight caching is done by the browser via `Access-Control-Max-Age`; `Vary` is about shared caches storing the main response.

options.text: The browser will refuse every response because `Vary` is mandatory in CORS
options.explanation: Browsers don't require `Vary`. It is a correctness requirement for caches, not a browser check.

questions.workedExample: A cache stores a response authorising app.example and reuses it for admin.example because Origin is not distinguished. Admin’s browser rejects the mismatched header. Vary: Origin enables correct variation in conforming caches when the response depends on Origin; preserve other Vary values too. It does not fix unsafe shared caching of user-specific content: use appropriate Cache-Control and authentication-aware cache policy. Correctly allowlisting origins plus missing Vary does not by itself authorise an untrusted origin.

questions.prompt: An internal API allowlists `Origin: null` "so that local HTML files used by the support team work". Why is this dangerous?

options.text: It isn't: only `file:` pages can send `Origin: null`
options.explanation: Sandboxed iframes and some redirect chains also produce `null`, and any website can create a sandboxed iframe.

options.text: An attacker's page can embed a sandboxed iframe whose requests carry `Origin: null`, so the allowlist effectively trusts any website
options.explanation: Correct as a trust-boundary flaw: distinct opaque origins serialize as null. Exposure of authenticated data additionally requires eligible credentials, suitable CORS credentials permission and a sensitive response.

options.text: `null` disables the preflight, so the attacker can send DELETE requests
options.explanation: The origin value doesn't change which requests are preflighted; that depends on method and headers.

options.text: Browsers convert `null` to `*`, which breaks credentials
options.explanation: Browsers do not rewrite the value. The danger is that the allowlist matches when it shouldn't, not a conversion.

questions.workedExample: A sandboxed iframe with allow-scripts but without allow-same-origin can execute with an opaque origin serialized as null. This gives an attacker a matching origin value if the API allowlists null. Reading private data additionally depends on credential eligibility, request mode and endpoint behaviour. Do not use null as the identity of a trusted support tool; serve it from a controlled named origin.

questions.prompt: Which statements about cross-origin behaviour are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A cross-origin `<script src>` runs with the including page's origin, so it can read that page's DOM
options.explanation: Correct. Script inclusion is code execution in your origin. That is why third-party scripts are a major trust decision.

options.text: Script can read the DOM of a cross-origin iframe if both pages are served over HTTPS
options.explanation: HTTPS doesn't grant access. Different host means different origin, so DOM access is blocked; the pages must use `postMessage`.

options.text: A receiver of `postMessage` should check `event.origin` before acting on the data
options.explanation: Correct. Also verify the expected source window when applicable and validate the payload structure. An untrusted window with a reference can send messages; checking origin alone does not make arbitrary data safe.

options.text: `https://a.example.com` and `https://b.example.com` are same-site but cross-origin
options.explanation: Correct. Hosts differ (cross-origin) but scheme and registrable domain `example.com` match (same-site).

options.text: Setting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` restrictively prevents CSRF
options.explanation: CORS headers only control whether responses can be read. Simple requests still arrive and take effect, so CSRF needs separate defences.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each claim using the read/write/embed split:

1. `<script src>` is embedding plus execution in *your* origin: true.
2. iframe DOM is a cross-origin *read*: blocked regardless of HTTPS.
3. `postMessage` deliberately crosses origins, so the receiver must authenticate the sender: true.
4. Origin compares full host; site compares eTLD+1: same-site, cross-origin, true.
5. CSRF is a *write*; CORS governs *reads*: false.

questions.prompt: A team allows `https://*.example.com` (any subdomain) with credentials on their account API. A pen-tester reports a reflected XSS on the forgotten `https://old-promo.example.com`. Assume a logged-in victim triggers the XSS, eligible API cookies are sent, and the API responds with sensitive data. What becomes possible?

options.text: Limited to the promo site, since XSS is confined to its own origin
options.explanation: The XSS is in the promo origin, but the API has granted that origin credentialed read access, so the impact spreads to the API.

options.text: An attacker can run script on the promo origin, call the account API with the victim's cookies and read the responses
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied conditions. Trusting the compromised origin grants access to the API responses that its credentials and authorisation permit, not automatically every resource.

options.text: None, because SameSite cookies stop subdomains sending cookies
options.explanation: The stated HTTPS sibling origins are same-site in an ordinary first-party context. SameSite alone therefore does not isolate them; cookie domain/path/expiry and other browser policy still matter.

options.text: The attacker can only send requests, not read them, because of the SOP
options.explanation: The CORS headers explicitly lift the SOP for that origin, so reads are allowed.

questions.workedExample: The injected script runs on the allowed promo origin, requests the account API with credentials mode include, and receives the sensitive response under the supplied cookie and server assumptions. CORS permits reading it. Narrow exact-origin allowlists and removal of unused subdomains reduce this trust surface; fixing XSS and server authorisation remain necessary.

questions.prompt: Assume a Chromium build whose preflight-cache maximum is 7,200 seconds. A successful preflight advertises Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400. What upper expiry bound follows, allowing earlier eviction?

options.text: 24 hours, exactly as requested
options.explanation: The supplied implementation cap is lower than the advertised value, so86400seconds is not the upper expiry bound.

options.text: Up to 2 hours, because Chromium caps the preflight cache
options.explanation: Correct. min(86400,7200)=7200 seconds, or two hours. Entries can be evicted sooner.

options.text: 5 seconds, because large values are ignored
options.explanation: 5 seconds is the default when the header is *absent*. A large value is clamped to the cap, not discarded.

options.text: Forever, until the user clears the cache
options.explanation: Preflight results are always time-limited; there's no permanent caching.

questions.workedExample: The supplied cap gives min(86400,7200)=7200seconds. Fetch permits an implementation cap and earlier removal; absent or invalid max-age defaults to5seconds in the standard. The checked Chromium source uses two hours, but future versions and other browsers require their own checks. A cached permission avoids an extra preflight only when its key and method/header conditions match.

lessons.title: XSS (stored, reflected, DOM) and CSP
lessons.summary: How attacker-controlled text ends up running as script in your users' browsers, why context-aware output encoding is the real fix, and how a strict Content Security Policy limits the damage when you miss one.
lessons.body:
The same-origin policy (lesson 1) protects one origin from another. **Cross-site scripting** (XSS) sidesteps it completely: the attacker gets their script to run *inside your origin*. From there it can do anything your own JavaScript can do: read the page, call your APIs with the user's cookies, change their email address, or show a fake login form on your real domain. In the OWASP Top10 2025 edition, XSS is covered by **A05 Injection**, because at heart it is the same bug as SQL injection: data is mixed into code without being kept separate. ## The core bug A web page is code (HTML, and JavaScript inside it). If you build that code by pasting in untrusted strings, some of those strings can change its structure. ```python @app.get("/search") def search(): q = request.args.get("q", "") # BAD: q is pasted into HTML return f"

Results for {q}

" ``` If `q` is `shoes`, the page says "Results for shoes". If `q` contains a `

questions.prompt: A forum saves each post's body to the database and inserts it directly into server-rendered HTML without encoding. A user's post contains script that runs for every reader. What type of XSS is this?

options.text: Reflected XSS
options.explanation: Reflected XSS echoes input from the *current request*. Here the payload was saved and served later to other users.

options.text: DOM-based XSS
options.explanation: Client-side sink insertion would make it DOM-based too, but this question specifies direct server rendering. Stored versus reflected is a different classification axis.

options.text: Stored XSS
options.explanation: Correct. The payload is persisted on the server and delivered to every viewer, with no crafted link needed.

options.text: Not XSS, because the attacker didn't send anything to the victim
options.explanation: XSS needs only that attacker-controlled data executes in the victim's browser in your origin. Stored XSS needs no direct contact with the victim.

questions.workedExample: The payload persists in the database and is delivered on later views, so it is stored XSS. Here the server inserts it into HTML. Persisted data inserted unsafely by client JavaScript could instead be both stored and DOM-based; URL data can also feed a DOM sink.

questions.prompt: What does `markupsafe.escape("Tom & Jerry")` produce?

options.text: `Tom & Jerry` unchanged, as it contains no script
options.explanation: Escaping is not script detection. It encodes every special HTML character regardless of whether the content looks dangerous.

options.text: `Tom & Jerry`, with the tags stripped
options.explanation: Stripping tags is what a sanitiser might do. Escaping keeps every character but makes it display as text.

options.text: `<b>Tom & Jerry</b>`
options.explanation: Correct. `<`, `>` and `&` become entities, so the browser shows the literal tags as text instead of making the text bold.

options.text: `%3Cb%3ETom%20%26%20Jerry%3C%2Fb%3E`
options.explanation: That is URL percent-encoding, which is for query strings, not HTML output. Using the wrong encoding for the context is a classic mistake.

link.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: Your session cookie is `HttpOnly`. A colleague says this means XSS on your site is no longer a serious risk. Why are they wrong?

options.text: `HttpOnly` cookies can still be read by `document.cookie` in older browsers only
options.explanation: All modern browsers enforce `HttpOnly`. The real issue is that the attacker doesn't need to read the cookie.

options.text: The injected script can still act as the user, sending requests from the page with the cookie attached automatically
options.explanation: Correct. HttpOnly blocks direct script access to the cookie, but eligible cookies can accompany same-origin requests. Server authorisation and reauthentication still determine which actions succeed.

options.text: `HttpOnly` only applies to HTTP, not HTTPS
options.explanation: That confuses `HttpOnly` (no script access) with `Secure` (HTTPS only). `HttpOnly` works on HTTPS too.

options.text: XSS can rewrite the cookie's flags
options.explanation: Non-HTTP cookie APIs cannot directly overwrite the matching HttpOnly cookie. Script may still invoke server endpoints that set cookies or affect sessions; direct cookie access is not required for serious harm.

questions.workedExample: HttpOnly prevents direct document.cookie access to that cookie. Injected script can still use allowed same-origin APIs with eligible ambient cookies and read responses. It can also read page data or present deceptive UI. Server permissions and reauthentication can limit actions; HttpOnly is useful but does not guarantee prevention of every form of session theft or abuse.

options.text: Yes, because all output is now escaped
options.explanation: The vulnerable output is produced by client JS, not the server. Server-side escaping never touches this value.

options.text: No: ordinary HTTP navigation omits the fragment, and this value reaches innerHTML in client code; use a text sink or suitable sanitisation
options.explanation: Correct for this data flow. Escaping server-rendered values never transforms the fragment before this sink. Replace innerHTML with textContent for ordinary text; server-supplied CSP can provide additional defence.

options.text: Yes, if they also add a WAF rule blocking `<script>` in URLs
options.explanation: A WAF never sees the fragment either, and `innerHTML` payloads don't need a `<script>` tag (event-handler attributes work).

options.text: No, because `decodeURIComponent` itself executes code
options.explanation: `decodeURIComponent` only decodes percent-escapes into a string. The sink, `innerHTML`, is the problem.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the data flow:

```
URL  /page#<payload>
      |  fragment stays in browser
      v
location.hash (source)
      |
      v
box.innerHTML (sink) -> parsed as HTML
```

No server-rendered value is on this source-to-sink path, so server-side output escaping misses it. Replace the sink:

```javascript
box.textContent = t;
```

Or, if HTML is genuinely needed, `box.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(t)`.

questions.prompt: A profile page renders a user-supplied website in a Jinja2 template with autoescaping on: ``` site ``` What is still a risk?

options.text: None: autoescaping covers attributes
options.explanation: Escaping stops breaking *out of* the attribute, but the value itself can be a dangerous URL. Escaping doesn't change `javascript:`.

options.text: A javascript: URL can remain dangerous on activation even though HTML escaping prevents breaking out of the attribute
options.explanation: Correct. URL attributes need scheme validation. Parse the URL and allow only `https:` (and perhaps `http:`/`mailto:`).

options.text: The double quotes in the template are unsafe; it should be unquoted
options.explanation: The opposite: quoted attributes are safer. Unquoted ones can be broken with a space.

options.text: Jinja2 doesn't escape inside tags
options.explanation: Jinja2's autoescape applies to every `{{ }}` expression, including inside attribute values; it escapes quotes so you can't break out.

questions.workedExample: Autoescaping prevents ordinary strings from breaking out of this quoted attribute, but does not validate URL semantics. A javascript: URL can still request script execution on activation, subject to browser/CSP checks. Use the platform’s URL parser and an application-specific scheme/destination policy, then still escape HTML output. Python urlparse only parses; it is not a complete browser-compatible URL security validator.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing a pull request in a React + Django codebase for XSS. Which of these deserve close scrutiny? Select all that apply.

options.text: `<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: bio}} />`
options.explanation: Correct. This bypasses JSX's automatic escaping; `bio` must be sanitised or provably trusted.

options.text:
`

{bio}

` in JSX
options.explanation: JSX escapes interpolated strings, so this renders as text. It's the safe default.

options.text: `{{ bio|safe }}` in a Django template
options.explanation: Correct. `|safe` tells Django the value is already safe HTML and disables autoescaping for it.

options.text: `mark_safe(f"{name}")` in a Django view
options.explanation: Correct. `name` is interpolated without escaping and then marked safe, so any HTML in it is rendered. Use `format_html` instead, which escapes the arguments.

options.text: `<a href={url}>` in JSX where `url` comes from the user
options.explanation: Correct as a URL-policy review point. React19 blocks javascript: URLs in src/href, unlike the older blanket claim. Framework protections do not replace application-specific allowed destinations/schemes or cover every version and custom component.

questions.workedExample: Look for places where escaping is switched off, or where escaping is the wrong tool: | Code | Why | |---|---| | dangerouslySetInnerHTML | escape hatch | | `{bio}` | auto-escaped, safe | | `\|safe` | escape hatch | | mark_safe(f-string) | unescaped input | | href={url} | URL context | Django's `format_html("{}", name)` is the safe way to build small HTML fragments: it escapes each argument before marking the result safe.

questions.prompt: A site sends `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-abc123'` with the **same nonce on every response**. Why is this weak?

options.text: Nonces must be at least 32 characters, so the browser ignores it
options.explanation: Browsers don't enforce a nonce length. The weakness is predictability, not format.

options.text: An attacker can read the nonce from any page and add it to their injected script tag
options.explanation: Correct. A nonce only works if the attacker can't know it in advance. A fixed value is visible in every page's source, so injected markup can include it.

options.text: It's fine: nonces are designed to be static per site
options.explanation: That describes an allowlist, not a nonce. A nonce ("number used once") must be fresh and unpredictable per response.

options.text: Static nonces disable `'strict-dynamic'`
options.explanation: The policy doesn't use `'strict-dynamic'`; and the issue is that the attacker can reuse the nonce, not a directive interaction.

questions.workedExample:
1. The point of a nonce: only scripts the *server* placed in this response know the value.
2. With a fixed nonce, the attacker loads any page, sees `nonce="abc123"` and puts it on the script element they inject.
3. The browser sees a matching nonce and runs it.
4. Fix: generate a new value per response, e.g. `secrets.token_urlsafe(16)` (128 bits), and make sure CDNs don't cache the HTML containing it.

link.title: Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP — web.dev

questions.prompt: You need to embed a server-side dictionary in a page for client JS. Which is the safest approach in Jinja2?

options.text: `<script>var cfg = {{ cfg }};</script>` relying on autoescape
options.explanation: Autoescape applies *HTML* encoding, which is wrong inside a script: it may corrupt the data and doesn't produce valid, safe JS.

options.text: `<script>var cfg = {{ cfg|safe }};</script>`
options.explanation: This inserts raw Python repr into JS with no encoding at all. A value containing `</script>` would end the block.

options.text: `<script>var cfg = {{ cfg|tojson }};</script>`
options.explanation: Correct. `tojson` produces valid JSON and escapes `<`, `>`, `&` and `'` so the value can't close the script tag.

options.text: `<script>var cfg = "{{ cfg }}";</script>` with quotes added
options.explanation: Wrapping in quotes doesn't make HTML escaping correct for JS, and you'd get a string rather than an object.

questions.workedExample: In an ordinary script element, raw data containing an HTML script-end sequence can terminate the element before JavaScript parsing. Jinja tojson serialises to JSON and escapes HTML-sensitive characters, including less-than, preventing that breakout. It is appropriate for the displayed object assignment. Its documentation also permits single-quoted attributes, but double-quoted attributes need additional handling. An enforced CSP still requires permission for the script that reads the data.

questions.prompt:
In a browser enforcing this CSP3 policy, with no other restrictions and the short nonce used only as a placeholder, which would the browser **block**? Select all that apply.

```
script-src 'nonce-R4nd'
  'strict-dynamic';
object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
```

options.text: `<script nonce="R4nd" src="/app.js">`
options.explanation: This carries the correct nonce, so it runs.

options.text: An inline `onclick="..."` attribute injected into a comment
options.explanation: Correct. Inline event handlers have no nonce and are blocked under a nonce-based policy.

options.text: An external script element with a src URL, dynamically created and appended by the authorised /app.js using document.createElement
options.explanation: This non-parser-inserted external script is permitted by strict-dynamic. Trusted loaders still need to avoid attacker-controlled script URLs.

options.text: An injected `<script src="https://cdn.example/x.js">` without a nonce
options.explanation: Correct. With `'strict-dynamic'`, host allowlists are ignored; only nonced scripts (and those they load) run.

options.text: An injected `<base href="https://evil.example/">`
options.explanation: Correct: base-uri none prevents the injected base URL from taking effect. It does not mean the DOM element itself cannot be inserted.

questions.workedExample: The matching nonce authorises the first script. The inline handler and unnonced parser-inserted external script are blocked. The specified dynamically created external script is allowed by strict-dynamic, while the injected base URL is rejected by base-uri none. The placeholder nonce must be replaced with fresh unpredictable entropy in real responses; trusted script gadgets remain relevant.

link.title: Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP — web.dev

questions.prompt: A site uses `script-src 'self' https://cdn.big-provider.com` (an allowlist). The CDN also hosts an old version of a popular framework with known script-gadget behaviour, and a JSONP endpoint. An attacker finds an HTML injection that can't run inline script. Why is the CSP likely ineffective?

options.text: Allowlists only apply to images
options.explanation: `script-src` governs scripts. The problem is what the allowed host serves.

options.text: The attacker can inject a `<script src>` pointing at something on the allowed CDN (a JSONP callback or a gadget-rich library) and turn it into code execution
options.explanation: Correct. Any allowed host that serves attacker-steerable script effectively allowlists the attacker. Google's 2016 study found most allowlist policies bypassable this way.

options.text: CSP is ignored on HTTPS sites
options.explanation: CSP works on HTTPS (that's the norm). Nothing about HTTPS disables it.

options.text: The attacker can override the CSP with a `<meta>` tag
options.explanation: A meta CSP can only add restrictions (policies combine by intersection); it cannot loosen the header policy.

questions.workedExample: An HTML injection may load an allowed external resource. If that endpoint or library has a usable attacker-controlled callback/gadget, execution can follow despite blocking inline scripts. Not every JSONP callback or old library provides such a bypass. A nonce/hash-based strict policy removes this host-allowlist path for unapproved parser-inserted scripts, but trusted loaders and gadgets still require review.

link.title: CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP! (Google research)

questions.prompt: A supporting browser enforces require-trusted-types-for script for a SPA. No default Trusted Types policy is configured. What changes for an ordinary string assigned to innerHTML?

options.text: It automatically sanitises every string assigned to `innerHTML`
options.explanation: Trusted Types doesn't sanitise anything itself; your policy decides what happens (often by calling DOMPurify).

options.text: Assigning a plain string to sinks like `innerHTML` throws; code must pass a `TrustedHTML` object created by a named policy
options.explanation: Correct. Only policies (a few auditable functions) can produce trusted values, so security review concentrates there instead of at every sink.

options.text: It disables `innerHTML` entirely
options.explanation: `innerHTML` still works with `TrustedHTML` values. Only raw strings are rejected.

options.text: It blocks all third-party scripts
options.explanation: That is `script-src`'s job. Trusted Types governs DOM injection sinks.

lessons.title: CSRF and SameSite
lessons.summary: Why browsers will happily send your users' cookies on requests that another site started, and the layered defences (tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin and Fetch Metadata checks) that stop it.
lessons.body:
The same-origin policy generally prevents a hostile page reading another origin’s responses, but does not prevent ordinary cross-origin form submissions. **Cross-site request forgery** (CSRF) exploits exactly that gap. The attacker can't see your bank's responses, but they don't need to. They only need the bank to *act* on a request.

## The attack

You are logged in to `bank.example`, which uses a session cookie. You visit `evil.example`, which contains a hidden form:

```
<form action=
  "https://bank.example/transfer"
  method="POST">
  <input name="to" value="attacker">
  <input name="amount" value="500">
</form>
<script>
  document.forms[0].submit()
</script>
```

The browser submits the form to the bank. If cookie scope, SameSite and other browser policies permit the session cookie, it accompanies the submission. A vulnerable endpoint accepts the predictable fields without an independent CSRF check or confirmation and performs the transfer.

```
 evil.example     browser         bank
     |  form       |                |
     |------------>|                |
     |             | POST /transfer |
     |             | Cookie: sid=.. |
     |             |--------------->|
     |             |     200 OK     |
     |             |<---------------|
                          money moves
```

The root cause: **possession of the session cookie does not establish user intent**. A server relying on that cookie alone cannot distinguish these requests.

### What CSRF can and cannot do

- It can trigger authorised actions when the attacker can construct accepted parameters and the endpoint lacks effective CSRF checks or additional confirmation.
- In the classic attack it is **blind**: SOP prevents reading the response. A separate CORS flaw, XSS or information leak can change that assumption.
- Classic authenticated CSRF exploits **ambient credentials** such as cookies sent automatically. An API accepting only a JavaScript-supplied bearer token avoids that mechanism if there is no ambient-authentication alternative. However, **client-side CSRF** can trick the legitimate application’s JavaScript into issuing an authenticated request using attacker-controlled input. Login CSRF also need not start with a logged-in victim.

> [!example] Login CSRF
> A twist: the attacker logs the victim into the *attacker's* account. The victim then saves a card or searches for something, and the attacker later sees it in their own account history. Login forms need CSRF protection too.

## Rule zero: GET must be safe

If `GET /transfer?to=attacker&amount=500` moves money, a link the victim clicks (or a redirect) is enough, and SameSite Lax won't help, because Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations (see below). An image request can also trigger an unsafe GET if the browser sends eligible credentials. HTTP defines GET, HEAD and OPTIONS as **safe**: their requested semantics must not perform the user’s state-changing operation. Incidental logging is permitted. Use POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE for such operations, with CSRF protection.

## Defence 1: anti-CSRF tokens

The **synchroniser token** pattern gives the legitimate page a secret that the attacker's page can't know:

1. When the session is created, the server generates a random token (a CSPRNG value, 128+ bits) and stores it in the session.
2. Legitimate state-changing forms and JS requests to the protected application include it in a hidden field or custom header. Never send it to an untrusted destination.
3. On every state-changing request, the server checks the submitted token matches the session's.

The attacker can make the browser send the cookie, but can't read your page to learn the token (the SOP blocks that read), so their forged request fails.

Vulnerable:

```python
@app.post("/transfer")
@login_required
def transfer():
    do_transfer(current_user,
                request.form["to"],
                request.form["amount"])
    return "ok"
```

Illustrative Flask hook (assumes `app`, `session`, `request` and `abort` are imported/configured). Render `csrf_token()` into protected forms and rotate the session/token at authentication boundaries. Flask’s default session is a signed client cookie, not a server-side session store. Prefer a maintained CSRF integration in production.

```python
import hmac, secrets

def csrf_token():
    if "csrf" not in session:
        session["csrf"] = \
            secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    return session["csrf"]

@app.before_request
def check_csrf():
    if request.method in (
            "GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
        return
    sent = (request.form.get("csrf")
        or request.headers.get(
            "X-CSRF-Token", ""))
    want = session.get("csrf")
    # no token in session: reject too,
    # or "" == "" would pass
    if (not isinstance(want, str)
            or not want
            or not want.isascii()
            or not sent.isascii()):
        abort(403)
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sent, want):
        abort(403)
```

`hmac.compare_digest` avoids content-dependent short-circuit comparison; type or length differences may still affect timing. Its string inputs must be ASCII, so the hook rejects non-ASCII input rather than raising an exception. Django’s generated project enables `CsrfViewMiddleware`; Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for unsafe methods. Check the framework integration and configuration used by your application.

### Double-submit cookies

If you can't keep server-side session state, the **double-submit** pattern puts the token in a cookie *and* in the request body or header, and checks they match. The attacker can't read the cookie to copy it into the form.

The naive version has a weakness: an attacker who controls any sibling subdomain (or a man-in-the-middle on plain HTTP) may be able to *set* a cookie for your domain, choosing both values. OWASP recommends the **signed** variant: bind a fresh random value and session-specific data into an HMAC with a server secret, and verify the signature as well as the submitted value. A valid token for another session must not work. In browsers enforcing cookie prefixes, `__Host-` forbids `Domain` and requires `Secure` and `Path=/`, preventing a sibling subdomain from planting that named parent-domain cookie. This does not isolate different ports on the same host.

## Defence 2: SameSite cookies

The `SameSite` cookie attribute tells the browser not to send a cookie on **cross-site** requests. Recall from lesson 1 that *site* means scheme + registrable domain, so `app.example.com` and `api.example.com` are same-site.

The following is a `Set-Cookie` value wrapped for display; join its lines with a space into one HTTP field value.

```
sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly;
SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

| Value | Cross-site requests that get the cookie |
|---|---|
| `Strict` | None at all |
| `Lax` | Top-level navigations with safe methods (clicking a link, a GET redirect) |
| `None` | SameSite imposes no restriction; other cookie policies still apply, and `Secure` is required |

So with `Lax`, the hidden-form POST from `evil.example` arrives **without** the session cookie, and the user appears logged out. With `Strict`, an initial navigation from a cross-site webmail page omits the cookie, so cookie-authenticated users can appear logged out on arrival; a common pattern is a `Lax` session cookie plus a `Strict` cookie required for sensitive actions.

### Browser defaults

Since 2020, Chrome (and other Chromium browsers) treat cookies **without** a `SameSite` attribute as `Lax`. Two caveats:

- To avoid breaking some single sign-on flows, Chrome makes an exception: a cookie without an explicit `SameSite` that is under **two minutes old** is still sent on top-level cross-site POSTs ("Lax+POST").
- Exact defaults and compatibility behavior are browser/version dependent. A verified Firefox/Safari version matrix is absent here; this lesson does not assert their current defaults.

So **set `SameSite` explicitly** rather than relying on the default.

```python
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax",
)
```

### Why SameSite alone isn't enough

- **Same-site attackers.** A compromised or taken-over subdomain (`old-blog.example.com`) is same-site with your app, so SameSite does nothing against it.
- **State-changing GETs.** `Lax` sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so a GET that transfers money is still exploitable.
- **Old or unusual clients** may not honour the attribute.

OWASP recommends explicit CSRF protection in most deployments, with SameSite as another layer. Its guidance describes constrained cases where SameSite can serve as the primary defence; those require careful conditions rather than a universal guarantee.

## Defence 3: checking where the request came from

Browsers add headers the attacker's page cannot forge:

- **`Origin`** is supplied for many relevant requests, but can be absent or serialise as `null`. Validate an exact trusted origin and define a safe policy for missing/opaque origins, using independent CSRF protection.
- **`Sec-Fetch-Site`** in supporting browsers reports `same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site` or `none` (for example, address-bar or bookmark navigation). Availability depends on the client and context. Arbitrary non-browser clients can forge these headers; they are not authentication.

```python
SAFE = {"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"}

@app.before_request
def fetch_metadata():
    site = request.headers.get(
        "Sec-Fetch-Site")
    if site is None:
        return  # still require token
    if request.method in SAFE:
        return
    if site not in ("same-origin",
                    "none"):
        abort(403)
```

This rejects many cross-site unsafe browser requests, but does not prevent same-origin XSS or client-side CSRF. Keep the token hook active independently, including when metadata is missing or `none`; the metadata policy is an additional filter.

## JSON APIs

A common belief is "our API takes JSON, so it's immune". It depends:

- If the server *requires* `Content-Type: application/json`, a cross-site request with that type is non-simple, so it is preflighted, and without permissive CORS the browser never sends it.
- If the server parses the body as JSON **regardless** of content type, an attacker can send a form with `enctype="text/plain"` crafted so the body happens to be valid JSON. That can be a simple request, delivered with any cookies allowed by browser policy.

So: check `Content-Type` strictly, or require a custom header such as `X-Requested-With` (which requires CORS preflight permission), and keep CORS tight.

## Related: clickjacking

Instead of forging a request, the attacker loads your real page in an invisible iframe and tricks the user into clicking a button on it. Tokens don't help, because the click happens on your genuine page. Prevent this framing with the `Content-Security-Policy` response header containing this policy value:

```
frame-ancestors 'none'
```

`frame-ancestors` is a CSP directive, not a standalone header. `X-Frame-Options: DENY` provides a legacy alternative. These controls address framing-based clickjacking; they do not prevent every form of deceptive UI.

## Evidence limits

A full browser/version compatibility matrix and live cross-browser attack testing are absent from this lesson. Browser-specific defaults must be checked for the supported clients; examples assume the credential and policy conditions stated above.

## Key takeaways
- Classic authenticated CSRF exploits eligible ambient credentials on attacker-triggered requests; SOP normally blocks response reads. Login CSRF and client-side CSRF require attention too.
- Keep GET safe. Protect every state-changing request, including login.
- Primary defence: framework anti-CSRF tokens (synchroniser, or signed double-submit). Compare in constant time.
- Set `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) explicitly; it doesn't stop same-site attackers or unsafe GETs.
- Check `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` as a cheap stateless layer. Require `application/json` or a custom header on APIs, and block framing with `frame-ancestors`.

## Further reading
- [Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [SameSite cookies explained — web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/samesite-cookies-explained)
- [Set-Cookie: SameSite — MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie)
- [Protect your resources with Fetch Metadata — web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/fetch-metadata)
- [Cross Site Request Forgery protection — Django docs](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/csrf/)
- [Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet — OWASP](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Clickjacking_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.prompt: Assume the browser permits the bank's session cookie on a cross-site form POST, and the transfer endpoint accepts predictable parameters without CSRF checks or additional confirmation. Why can evil.example trigger a transfer?

options.text: Because the attacker has stolen the user's session cookie
options.explanation: CSRF doesn't need the cookie value. The browser attaches it by itself; the attacker never sees it.

options.text: The browser attaches an eligible session cookie to the cross-site form submission, and SOP does not prevent that submission
options.explanation: Correct. Possession of the ambient session credential does not establish user intent.

options.text: Because the bank's CORS policy allows `evil.example`
options.explanation: CORS controls reading responses. A form POST is a simple request that goes out without any CORS permission.

options.text: Because the bank's site has an XSS vulnerability
options.explanation: XSS is a different bug (script in the bank's origin). CSRF works from the attacker's own site with no bug in the bank's HTML.

questions.workedExample:
1. The user logged in earlier, so the browser holds `sid` for `bank.example`.
2. `evil.example` serves an auto-submitting form targeting `bank.example/transfer`.
3. Form submissions to other origins are allowed (they're writes).
4. With all applicable cookie policies permitting it, the browser includes `Cookie: sid=...`.
5. The bank sees an authenticated, valid request and acts.

The attacker never reads anything, which is why CSRF is called blind.

link.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: An app deletes a user's account with `GET /account/delete`. Why is this especially bad for CSRF?

options.text: A single click on an attacker's link (or a redirect) triggers it, because `SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations
options.explanation: Correct. GET is supposed to be safe; making it state-changing means ordinary links and redirects trigger it, and Lax cookies are sent on those. With `SameSite=None` cookies, even an image tag would do.

options.text: GET requests are always sent without cookies
options.explanation: GETs carry cookies like any other request (subject to SameSite). That's why this is dangerous.

options.text: GET requests can't carry CSRF tokens
options.explanation: Tokens can appear in query strings but risk exposure in logs and, depending on referrer policy, Referer headers. Use an unsafe method for the operation and retain CSRF protection.

options.text: GET is fine as long as the response is JSON
options.explanation: The response format is irrelevant: CSRF doesn't need to read the response; the deletion has already happened.

questions.workedExample: 1. HTTP defines GET as safe: no requested state-changing operation (incidental logging is allowed). 2. Browsers issue GETs everywhere: images, prefetches, links, previews. 3. `` cross-site is a subresource, so `Lax` cookies aren't sent; but a link click or a redirect is a top-level navigation, and `Lax` *does* send cookies then. 4. So a single click on an attacker link deletes the account. Fix: `POST /account/delete` (or `DELETE`) with a CSRF token.

questions.prompt: A user follows a top-level link from a cross-site HTTPS webmail page to https://shop.example/orders. Authentication relies solely on a SameSite=Strict session cookie. What happens on that initial request?

options.text: The cookie is sent, because clicking a link is a user action
options.explanation: That's `Lax` behaviour. `Strict` withholds the cookie on *every* cross-site request, including top-level link clicks.

options.text: The browser blocks the navigation
options.explanation: SameSite never blocks requests; it only controls whether the cookie is attached.

options.text: The request arrives without the cookie, so the user appears logged out on landing
options.explanation: Correct. The initial cross-site navigation omits the Strict cookie. Do not assume that a browser reload necessarily changes its SameSite classification.

options.text: The cookie is sent only if the link uses HTTPS
options.explanation: `Secure` controls HTTPS-only sending; `SameSite` is about the request's initiating site.

questions.workedExample:
1. Initiator: webmail site (cross-site). Target: `shop.example`.
2. `Strict` → cookie omitted on any cross-site request.
3. Server sees an anonymous request → login page or logged-out view.
4. This UX cost is why many sites use `Lax` for the main session cookie, sometimes plus a separate `Strict` cookie checked only for sensitive actions.

questions.prompt: The session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax`. Which cross-site requests from `evil.example` to `app.example` will include it? Assume all other cookie conditions permit sending, the link and location examples navigate the top-level window, and no redirects intervene. Select all that apply.

options.text: An auto-submitted hidden `<form method="POST">`
options.explanation: Lax withholds cookies on cross-site POSTs. (The Lax+POST exception applies only to cookies with *no* SameSite attribute.)

options.text: The user clicking `<a href="https://app.example/x">`
options.explanation: Correct. A top-level navigation with a safe method gets `Lax` cookies.

options.text: ``
options.explanation: Images are subresource requests, not top-level navigations, so Lax cookies aren't sent.

options.text: `fetch("https://app.example/api", {credentials: "include"})`
options.explanation: A cross-site fetch is not a top-level navigation; Lax cookies are withheld even with `credentials: "include"`.

options.text: `window.location = "https://app.example/y"` (GET)
options.explanation: Correct. Script-initiated top-level GET navigation is still a top-level safe navigation, so Lax cookies go.

questions.workedExample:
Lax rule: send on cross-site requests **only** if top-level navigation **and** safe method.

| Request | Top-level? | Safe? | Sent |
|---|---|---|---|
| form POST | yes | no | no |
| link click | yes | yes | yes |
| img | no | yes | no |
| fetch | no | yes | no |
| location= | yes | yes | yes |

So Lax stops the classic POST CSRF but not unsafe GET endpoints.

questions.prompt:
Trace this CSRF check when the session has **no** `csrf` key yet and the attacker's form sends no token:

```python
sent = request.form.get("csrf", "")
if not hmac.compare_digest(
        sent,
        session.get("csrf", "")):
    abort(403)
```

options.text: 403: a missing token is always rejected
options.explanation: Trace it: both sides default to the empty string, and `compare_digest("", "")` is True, so `abort` is never reached.

options.text: The request passes: both values are `""`, which compare equal
options.explanation: Correct. Defaults on both sides collapse to the same value. The check must reject when the expected token is missing.

options.text: `compare_digest` raises a TypeError on empty strings
options.explanation: It accepts empty strings fine and returns True when both are empty.

options.text: The request passes only if the user is logged in
options.explanation: This snippet has no login check at all; the result is the same either way.

questions.workedExample:
Both missing values default to the empty string; compare_digest("", "") is True, so the vulnerable check passes. Reject missing expected values and non-ASCII strings before comparison:

```python
want = session.get("csrf")
if (not isinstance(want, str)
        or not want
        or not want.isascii()
        or not sent.isascii()):
    abort(403)
if not hmac.compare_digest(sent, want):
    abort(403)
```

Here sent is the form string from the question. The ASCII guard also prevents a TypeError on hostile Unicode input.

link.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: An SPA's API accepts only an Authorization bearer token held in JS memory, with no alternative ambient authentication. Assume no XSS, token leak or client-side confused-deputy behavior. Can a hostile site's direct cross-site request perform classic authenticated CSRF?

options.text: Yes: any API that changes state needs a CSRF token
options.explanation: CSRF tokens defend against *ambient* credentials. Here the credential isn't ambient, so there's nothing for the attacker's page to ride on.

options.text: No: the browser never adds the bearer token automatically, so a forged cross-site request arrives unauthenticated
options.explanation: Correct. The attacker's page can't read the token (different origin) and the browser won't attach it, so forged requests fail authentication.

options.text: No, but only because the API uses JSON
options.explanation: JSON alone doesn't protect a cookie-based API (text/plain tricks). Here the reason is the non-ambient credential.

options.text: Yes, if the user has another tab open on the SPA
options.explanation: Other tabs don't share the in-memory token with the attacker's page; the SOP prevents that.

questions.workedExample: The browser does not automatically attach the token to a request made by the hostile page, so that request fails authentication. This does not prove the SPA immune to client-side CSRF: attacker-controlled input could cause the legitimate app to send an authenticated request. XSS and token theft remain separate risks.

link.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: A state-changing request arrives with `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site`. Your app is `https://app.example.com`. Using the Fetch Metadata policy from the lesson (allow only `same-origin` and `none` for unsafe methods), what should happen, and why does it matter?

options.text: Allow it: same-site means it came from your own site
options.explanation: Same-*site* includes every subdomain of `example.com`, such as a forgotten marketing subdomain. That's exactly the gap SameSite cookies leave.

options.text: Reject it under the stated policy: same-site is not the allowed same-origin or none value
options.explanation: Correct. A sibling subdomain can be same-site while being a different origin. The header is a browser request-context signal, not proof of authentication or user intent; non-browser clients can forge it.

options.text: Reject it: `same-site` is only sent by old browsers
options.explanation: Supporting browsers can report same-site for cross-origin same-site contexts. Missing headers can reflect client or context differences, not just age; redirect history can also affect classification.

options.text: Allow it, but only if the method is POST
options.explanation: POST is the dangerous case. The method doesn't change whether the initiator is trusted.

questions.workedExample:
1. `Sec-Fetch-Site` values: `same-origin` (exact origin), `same-site` (e.g. `blog.example.com` → `app.example.com`), `cross-site`, `none` (typed URL/bookmark).
2. The policy accepts only `same-origin` and `none`.
3. `same-site` → 403.
4. Why it matters: if `blog.example.com` is taken over, SameSite cookies still flow (same site). Fetch Metadata can tell the difference; SameSite can't.

If you genuinely have cross-origin callers on your own domain, allowlist them explicitly.

link.title: Protect your resources with Fetch Metadata — web.dev

questions.prompt: A cookie-authenticated API endpoint does `data = json.loads(request.get_data())` without checking `Content-Type`. CORS is locked down. Assume cookies are eligible, there is no independent CSRF check, and the accepted schema can be encoded by the crafted form. How could an attacker still mount CSRF?

options.text: They can't: JSON requests are always preflighted
options.explanation: The body being JSON does not itself trigger preflight. application/json is not a CORS-safelisted request content type; other method/header conditions can also require permission.

options.text: Submit a cross-site form with `enctype="text/plain"` whose body happens to parse as JSON; it's a simple request, sent with cookies
options.explanation: Correct. `text/plain` is a safelisted type, so no preflight; the lenient server parses the body as JSON anyway.

options.text: Use `fetch` with `mode: "no-cors"` and `Content-Type: application/json`
options.explanation: `no-cors` mode only allows safelisted content types; the browser won't send `application/json` in that mode.

options.text: Read the CORS policy and copy an allowed origin into the `Origin` header
options.explanation: Pages can't set the `Origin` header; the browser sets it. That's why it is useful for defence.

questions.workedExample:
1. Preflight is triggered by a non-safelisted `Content-Type`, not by the body's shape.
2. A form with `enctype="text/plain"` sends `name=value` pairs joined in a way an attacker can arrange to look like a JSON object.
3. The request is simple → no preflight → cookies attached (subject to SameSite).
4. The server ignores `Content-Type` and parses JSON successfully.

Defences:
- Reject anything not `application/json`.
- Require a custom header with a restrictive CORS policy (requires preflight permission, which may be cached).
- Check `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-Site`, and use SameSite.

link.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: A naive double-submit scheme checks equality between a cookie and a submitted value. Its normal JS client reads the cookie into a header; the server also accepts the value in a form field. Which changes strengthen it against cookie injection or network attackers? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authenticate a random token together with session-specific binding data using an HMAC with a server secret, and verify it
options.explanation: Correct. A session-bound signed double-submit token prevents an attacker choosing a valid value for another session.

options.text: Name the cookie with the `__Host-` prefix
options.explanation: Correct. `__Host-` cookies must be `Secure`, have `Path=/` and no `Domain`, so a sibling subdomain can't set or overwrite them.

options.text: Make the CSRF cookie `HttpOnly`
options.explanation: The app's own JS needs to read the cookie to copy it into the header, so `HttpOnly` breaks the pattern. And it doesn't stop cookie *injection*.

options.text: Serve the whole site over HTTPS with HSTS
options.explanation: Correct. HTTPS prevents HTTP response injection on protected connections. HSTS helps when its policy is already known or preloaded; an unprotected first visit and uncovered subdomains remain deployment concerns.

options.text: Make the token longer (256 bits instead of 128)
options.explanation: The weakness is the attacker *setting* both values, not guessing them. Length doesn't help.

questions.workedExample: Cookie injection alone does not let a hostile page set a custom request header through restrictive CORS. Here the server additionally accepts a form token, letting an attacker submit the planted value. Bind the signed token to the authenticated session and random nonce. A browser-enforced __Host- prefix prevents sibling-domain injection of that named cookie. HTTPS plus known/preloaded HSTS addresses network injection, subject to host coverage. HttpOnly would break the stated JS cookie-reading client; making an already-unpredictable token longer does not address injection.

link.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet — OWASP

questions.prompt: Assume a Chromium configuration with Lax-by-default and the 120-second Lax-allowing-unsafe exception. A session cookie with no SameSite attribute was newly created 60 seconds ago. A malicious page now submits a top-level cross-site POST; all other cookie conditions permit sending. Is the cookie sent?

options.text: No: Chrome treats missing SameSite as Lax, which never sends cookies on cross-site POSTs
options.explanation: Lax-by-default has a temporary exception for fresh cookies. Missing it is a common misunderstanding.

options.text: Yes: Chrome's Lax+POST exception sends cookies under two minutes old (without an explicit SameSite) on top-level cross-site POSTs
options.explanation: Correct. The cookie is 60 s old, under the 2-minute window, so it's sent. Setting `SameSite=Lax` explicitly removes the exception.

options.text: Yes: cookies without SameSite are always treated as `None`
options.explanation: Not under the stated configuration: missing SameSite uses a default mode with a limited recent-cookie exception, rather than unrestricted None behavior.

options.text: No: Chrome blocks all cross-site POST form submissions
options.explanation: Chrome doesn't block form submissions; SameSite only controls cookies.

questions.workedExample: Under the stated configuration, the newly created cookie is 60 seconds old, inside the assumed 120-second window, and the request is a top-level navigation. The cookie is sent. Explicit SameSite=Lax does not get this default-mode exception. Cookie creation time matters; a later replacement does not necessarily reset it. Maintain independent CSRF protection and check supported-client behavior.

questions.prompt: The authenticated delete-account page loads in a cross-site iframe because browser cookie policies permit it. It contains a valid CSRF token. An attacker overlays its transparent iframe on a decoy prize button so a click hits the real delete control. In a browser enforcing the response policies below, which defence prevents this framing attack?

options.text: Rotating the CSRF token on every request
options.explanation: The click happens on your genuine page, which includes a valid token. Token rotation doesn't matter.

options.text: `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`)
options.explanation: Correct. These response headers prevent the page being embedded in the described frame; they do not eliminate every form of deceptive UI.

options.text: Nothing extra: the CSRF token already prevents it
options.explanation: The genuine framed page submits its valid token. Possession of that token does not prove the user understood or intended the action.

options.text: A strict `script-src` CSP
options.explanation: No attacker script runs on your page; `script-src` is irrelevant. `frame-ancestors` is the CSP directive that matters.

questions.workedExample:
1. Clickjacking isn't a forged request: the user really clicks your real button inside a hidden frame.
2. The framed page was rendered by your server, so its CSRF token is valid.
3. Under the question’s assumptions, browser policies permit the session cookie in this iframe. SameSite=None alone does not guarantee this; third-party-cookie restrictions can still block it. (With `Lax` or `Strict` the frame would load logged out, which is one reason those are safer defaults.)
4. The real control: tell the browser never to render your page in someone else's frame.

```
frame-ancestors 'none'
```

Or `'self'` if you frame yourself, or list the partner origins for the widget pages only.
